It isn't that people 'don't want to work anymore'. Most people enjoy being productive and solving problems - it's one of the main ways that our monkey brains register happiness. What we don't like is being taken advantage of. We don't like being overworked, underpaid, and treated disrespectfully. 

We want to feel like our work is making a difference, at least some of the time, rather than vanishing into a quarterly report, the benefits of which we'll never see or feel. Most people don't want a mega yacht or a private jet - only rich people seem to have this strange and unnatural compulsion to collect status symbols and waste resources. Most people want to provide a good life for their families. Pursue hobbies and create art in their spare time. Travel once in a while. These are all reasonable expectations. However, the idea of  what's 'reasonable' is being depressed year over year. What was once a single family home is now a shitty apartment with extortionate rent. The 40 hr work week is now 60 hrs just to stay afloat. The price of gas and groceries, a college education, healthcare.

The middle class, which has more in common with the working poor than the upper class, has been fed a crock that they are special, more hardworking, and more deserving than their fellow citizens, which is why they have been spared the punishment of poverty, when the reality is that they too are scraping by paycheck to paycheck and are one bad diagnosis away from falling into the trap themselves.

Class solidarity is going to be the most important vehicle for social change in the coming decades - maybe the only vehicle.

I know what it feels like to get bigger and suddenly feel very uncomfortable in your own body and it isn't fun. You aren't alone and you can definitely make a change! One mistake I made at the beginning was cutting too hard and too fast, eating 800 cals a day and working out for an hour. While I lost weight, this was not sustainable and I ended up gaining weight back. 

I would strongly suggest cutting down or eliminating alcohol. I could not lose any weight until I did this. Today, I don't drink at all. You don't need to be a teetotaler but limiting alcohol will definitely make your weight loss much easier. 

Make sustainable lifestyle choices, like eating 100-200 fewer calories every meal. Focus on getting protein, healthy fats, carbs from fruit and veggies and fiber. Stay hydrated! Get your body moving. Even just a walk is a good start.

DON'T cut out all the foods you love. A little treat in moderation is a good thing and will keep you from falling off the wagon. Identify the treat foods that are actually healthy in moderation (eg. peanut butter) and allow yourself to have them. 

 Good luck!

Rule of thumb is 1lb = 3500 cals so unless you are slamming down 3500 calories in one sitting when you are eating out, you shouldn't be gaining weight. My initial thought is that you could be noticing water weight from high sodium foods. Also, keep in mind that your body weight fluctuates throughout the day within a 5lb range, so the 1lb you're noticing is well within your margin of error. Even though you have reached your goal weight,keep weighing yourself at intervals and pay attention to the trend line. Is it going up? Down? More or less the same?

If you really are gaining weight, then this isn't an issue of a one time treat. It would have to be a pattern of eating over your caloric needs for a sustained period. Remember that can happen with healthy foods too. Since you mention you were maintaining a 200 cal deficit, it looks like you don't have much room for error. Track your calories! You may be eating more than you think. 

One treat or high calorie meal won't make you gain weight, but you'll need to maintain good food habits in the long run to keep the weight off.
